title: min, abs, and round make numbers easier to read
when_to_show: When finding the minimum value in a list of numbers or reading the difference or the rounded result
body: min selects the smallest value, abs returns an absolute value, and round returns a rounded value.
detail: They do not mutate the input, but min([]) raises ValueError and binary floating-point rounding may differ from an intuitive decimal rule. Check input type, emptiness, and how the result is used.

title: `any` and `isinstance` are tools for checking conditions.
when_to_show: When checking whether any of the conditions in the list is true or verifying the type of a value
body: `any` and `isinstance` are commonly used tools for checking conditions. `any` evaluates the entire expression to `True` if any one of several conditions is `True`.
detail: For example, `any(x > 10 for x in nums)` checks whether there is at least one value greater than 10 in `nums`. `isinstance(value, int)` checks whether `value` is of the `int` data type. When reading code, look first at the loop condition inside `any` and determine which condition, if any, needs to be satisfied. `isinstance` frequently appears in input validation, function argument checks, and branching logic between strings and numbers.

title: `startswith`, `endswith`, and `find` check the position and format of a string
when_to_show: When checking file names, prefixes, suffixes, and locations
body: `startswith`, `endswith`, and `find` are tools for checking the structure and position of a string.
detail: `startswith` returns `True` or `False` depending on whether a string begins with a specific character, and `endswith` returns `True` or `False` depending on whether it ends with a specific character. `find` returns the position where the target string first appears as a number; if it is not found, it returns -1. When reading code, note that `startswith` and `endswith` are often used directly in conditional statements, while `find` is frequently used to determine positions for slicing or branching decisions. For example, `filename.endswith(".json")` checks for a file extension, and `url.startswith("https://")` checks for a valid URL format.

title: An f-string embeds a variable's value within a string
when_to_show: When outputting a string that contains variable values
body: An f-string is a syntax that naturally embeds variable values into a string.
detail: When you use curly braces ({}) within a string prefixed with an "f"—such as {name} or {count}—the current value of the variable or the result of a simple calculation is inserted in that position. When reading code, it’s easier to distinguish between characters that remain as-is within the quotes and parts that are evaluated within the curly braces. For example, `f"{user}, {score} points"` reads the current values of `user` and `score` to construct a single string. F-strings are frequently used in `print` output, log messages, filename generation, API response messages, and error messages.

title: `list.pop` removes a value from the list while retrieving it.
when_to_show: When retrieving the last value or a value at a specific position from a list
body: list.pop returns and removes the item at an index, using the last item when no index is supplied. An empty list or out-of-range index raises IndexError.
detail: Track the list before the call, the returned item, and the list afterward.

title: `setdefault` and `dict.pop` modify the state of the dictionary
when_to_show: When setting a default value in a dictionary or removing a key
body: Both `setdefault` and `dict.pop` are tools that can modify the state of a dictionary. `setdefault(key, default_value)` sets the default value if the key does not exist and returns that value.
detail: If the key already exists, it does not set the new default value but simply returns the existing value. This is why it’s often seen in the “create if it doesn’t exist, use the existing one if it does” pattern. `dict.pop(key)` removes the value associated with that key from the dictionary. Just like `pop` in a list, it returns a value, so you can store the retrieved value in another variable, such as `removed = data.pop("old")`.

title: Distinguish between discard, intersection, difference, and set comprehension
when_to_show: When safely removing elements from a set or identifying similarities and differences
body: A set is a collection of unique values. While a list prioritizes order and position, a set focuses on which values are included and on removing duplicates.
detail: `discard` is a safe removal tool that removes a value without raising an error even if the value is absent. `intersection` finds the common values between two sets, while `difference` finds values present in one set but not in the other. A set comprehension is a syntax for creating a new set using loops and conditions, similar to a list comprehension.

title: `readline` and `readlines` read files line by line.
when_to_show: When looking at code that reads the first line or multiple lines from a file,
body: You’ll often encounter `readline` and `readlines` when creating a workflow to read a file line by line.
detail: While `read()` fetches the entire file as a single large string, `readline()` reads only one line from the current position and moves on to the next line. This makes them a natural choice for creating a “read one line, check it, and store only the necessary values” workflow within a loop. Since `readlines()` retrieves multiple lines as a list, it’s convenient for quickly reviewing configuration files or sample data that don’t contain many lines. When reading code, you should first determine whether the file is read all at once, whether a list of lines is created, or whether it is processed line by line in a loop.

title: "global" indicates that the variable outside the function will be modified directly.
when_to_show: When you see code that modifies an outer variable from within a function
body: The `global` keyword indicates that you intend to directly modify a variable outside the function. At the beginner level, it’s more important to read code carefully than to use `global` frequently.
detail: If you write something like `count = count + 1` inside a function, Python typically treats `count` as a local variable within that function. However, if `global count` is present, it means the function intends to directly modify the outer `count`. When reading code, as soon as you see `global`, you should assume that the value of the outer variable may change even after the function has finished executing. While this might seem convenient in small examples, it becomes difficult to track where values have changed as the code grows.
